payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
A recording is delivered once and then holds still. Remasters and radio edits exist, but each is a separate artifact with its own identity rather than a revision of the original. Nothing overwrites what was delivered.

That makes music unusual among digital objects carrying financial weight. Contracts get amended, filings get corrected, and published writing gets updated whenever the surrounding material shifts under it. A master accumulates none of that motion. It arrives complete, and the only thing that happens afterward is distribution. Session files and stems may survive somewhere, on a studio drive or in an archive nobody maintains, but those are private, unversioned, and easy to alter without leaving a mark. They carry little standing when a claim is made against the released work years later.

Immutability removes the trail, not the dispute

An artifact that never changes has no revision history, so a dispute arriving years later cannot be settled by consulting one. No prior state exists to compare the current one against.

Systems built around mutable documents can afford to be relaxed about the moment of creation, because evidence accrues as the object moves through the world. Each amendment leaves a mark, and enough marks add up to a history somebody can reconstruct later. That reconstruction is doing real work, and it is available precisely because the object kept moving.

Music offers no such accumulation. When the question arrives, and it usually arrives as a royalty claim or an authorship challenge rather than an abstract inquiry, the record either exists from the beginning or it does not exist at all. Nothing in the intervening years produced one.

The window closes at delivery

Detection approaches this from the far end. Given a finished file, it estimates what produced the file, which is reconstruction after the fact from the only thing still available. For an object that has been amended and annotated and versioned, that reconstruction has surrounding material to lean on. For a master, the artifact is the whole of the evidence, and the artifact is silent about its own origin.

This is why binding at creation carries so much weight in music specifically. The moment of creation is the last point at which anything true about origin can attach to the file, because the file will never again be in a state where new evidence naturally accrues to it. Sign it then, and the claim travels with the artifact for as long as the artifact exists. Miss that window and there is no second one.

The property this buys is narrow and worth stating plainly. A record made at creation is available at dispute time without anyone having to reconstruct it. That is a different kind of claim from an estimate produced years later by a model examining a waveform, and the difference shows up the moment either one has to hold up in front of a party with money at stake.

The catalog was finished before any of this

The uncomfortable part is what this implies backward. Everything already released was made without such a record, and no amount of later analysis creates one. That material is not a transitional problem waiting for better tooling. It is a permanent class of work whose origins were never captured and cannot be captured now, which is a distinct problem from the one facing work that has not been made yet.

The volume of that catalog is the reason the argument keeps getting made in the wrong direction. Detection promises coverage of everything that already exists, which is genuinely the larger pile. What it cannot do is produce the one thing a dispute actually needs, which is a record that was there from the start.
payload.title: The master never moves
